title: Solar shower
summary: Heat water in a black container or coil of black hose in the sun, raise it above head height and let gravity run a shower. A 20 L drum in summer sun reaches a comfortable 35–45 °C by afternoon; a hose coil can get dangerously hot. Not for drinking.

materials.item: Dark container that never held fuel or chemicals: drum, jerrycan or water bag, 10–40 L (or 20–30 m of black garden hose)
Black garden hose for a coil heater
Tap or valve at the outlet
Hose from tap to shower head
Shower head: watering-can rose, or a bottle cap with 10–20 small holes
Matt black paint for light-coloured containers
Clear glazing (glass or clear plastic) for a warm box around the container
Insulation behind the container in a box
Stand: timber or steel, strong enough for the full container

steps.text: Pick a container that never held chemicals, fuel or poisons. Clean it well. Paint the outside matt black if it isn't dark already.
Fit a tap at the lowest point and a short hose to a shower head. Seal the fittings with washers on both sides.
Optional: set the container in a shallow box with insulation behind and clear glass or plastic in front. It heats faster and still works in cool, sunny weather.
Build or choose a stand that puts the container 1.5–2.2 m off the ground, above head height. Brace it so it can't tip.
steps.warn: Water weighs 1 kg per litre: a 40 L container is 40 kg overhead. A weak stand can drop it on someone.

steps.text: Fill it in the morning and face it into the sun. Lift it into place full only if you can do it safely; otherwise fill it in place with a hose or bucket from a ladder.
steps.warn: Lifting a heavy full container overhead strains backs and drops loads. Fill it in place or use a pulley.

steps.text: Before showering, run a little water onto your wrist. Mix with cold water if it's too hot.
steps.warn: Water from a black hose coil can pass 60 °C on a hot day and scalds in seconds. Always test first.

steps.text: Shower: wet down, turn off, soap up, turn on to rinse. About 5–10 L does one person.
Drain what's left at the end of the day and refill fresh. Let used water soak away onto plants or a gravel pit, well away from wells and streams.

notes:
## Heating maths
Energy to heat water: 1.16Wh per litre per °C.
- 20 L from 15 °C to 40 °C: 20 × 25 × 1.16 ≈ 580Wh.
- Strong sun gives about 800W per m². A dark container showing 0.5 m² to the sun, catching about half of that, gains about 200W: roughly 3 hours to heat 20 L by 25 °C.
- Clouds, wind and cold air slow it. A glazed box halves the losses.

## Hose coil
A black hose coiled flat on a dark roof heats fast because it holds little water: 30 m of 13 mm hose holds only about 4 L. It's ideal for a quick hand wash or a short shower, but can reach scalding temperatures by midday.

## Germs
Warm water left standing for days (25–45 °C) can grow bacteria, including the kind that causes Legionnaires' disease when breathed in as spray. Use water within a day, drain the container, and let it dry and get hot and empty now and then. Shower water isn't drinking water.

## Pressure
Each metre of height gives about 0.1 bar. At 2 m you get a gentle flow, enough with a fine rose. For more, use a garden pressure sprayer as a pump shower: fill with warm water, pump, spray.

## Variations
- Several black drums in a glazed box on the roof can heat 100–200 L for a household.
- Pre-warm a water heater tank's inlet water this way to save fuel.
- Use the same setup to heat washing-up water.

## If you lack a part
- No tap: a hose clamp on the outlet hose works as a valve.
- No stand: hang the container from a branch or roof beam with a strap rated for the weight, or use a pulley to lift it.
